answers.answer: Caching could avoid repeatedly building the same popular guide in the database: a usable hit takes the 2 ms cache lookup instead of the 80 ms database work. Weekly changes suggest reuse is useful, provided the team defines acceptable staleness. Use station:{stationID}:language:{language}, so English and Spanish never share a result. On a hit the API reads the cache and returns its guide; a hit alone does not prove freshness. On a miss the API reads/builds the guide from the database, writes a copy to the cache, and returns it. The cache does not fetch it itself. A miss still pays the cache lookup, the 80 ms database work, and cache write cost. Caching also adds storage and work to keep copies current. The database retains the durable source record.

evidence.quote: Include the inputs that change the answer.
No usable entry exists. The application reads the database, stores a copy in the cache and returns the result.
Storage, lookups and keeping copies current all have costs.

answers.answer: C receives the old hours. B deleted the key before A wrote its already-fetched old value back, so deletion did not prevent a later stale refill. The team cannot claim every read after B finishes sees new hours: C is a counterexample. For an endpoint requiring the latest committed hours, have the API read the authoritative database directly on each request instead of serving this cached copy. In the stated sequence that returns the new committed hours. No concurrency protocol is needed for this proposed bypass.

evidence.quote: A reader can fetch $20 before the update, pause, then refill $20 after removal. The next cache hit still returns $20.
Keep freshness-critical decisions tied to authoritative data.

answers.answer: Case A: at 12:03 the original entry is still usable and can return the old forecast despite the 12:02 source change. At 12:11 it has expired, so the API must fetch the source and can cache the fetched result. Case B: at 12:05 the entry is absent after the 12:04 removal, so the API must fetch the source even though ten minutes have not passed. The TTL limits this entry's lifetime to ten minutes from storage; it does not promise freshness after a source change, automatic refresh at 12:10, or that the entry will stay available for all ten minutes. Removing it for memory is eviction, a capacity decision, whereas expiration is reaching its allowed lifetime.

evidence.quote: Sets how long an entry may remain before it expires.
An entry can be evicted before its TTL ends.
TTL limits an entry's lifetime, not the age of the source data used to fill it.

answers.answer: Use one shared cache entry as the simpler fit for this goal. Today each local lookup happens inside the instance handling the request, and each instance manages its own copy. Deleting the writer instance's copy leaves the other three copies untouched, so requests routed to those instances can return an old map; the writer instance can miss and refill the new map. With the stated single shared entry and no concurrent fills, all four instances look up the same entry across the network in a separate service. Deleting it makes subsequent lookups miss for every instance, letting the application reload from the database. This adds the acceptable 2 ms network lookup and a service to operate. Losing one local cache affects only its own instance; the other three retain theirs. An unreachable shared cache denies cached access to all four instances. Sharing alone does not keep the entry current with the database.

evidence.quote: Several API servers use a separate cache service, such as Redis or Memcached.
Restarting one API process discards its local cache; other processes keep their copies.
If the shared cache is unreachable, every API server using it loses access to those cached entries.

answers.answer: Expiration can make many simultaneous requests miss the same schedule and each start the same database read, overwhelming its 500 reads/second capacity. Coalesce readers for that key: let one application lookup fetch the schedule, have concurrent requests share that in-progress lookup, then return its result and fill the cache. This replaces repeated reads with one read for the group; coordination must cover the requests sharing that lookup, and the lesson does not specify its implementation across instances. A full outage can turn nearly all 10,000 requests/second into database reads for a minute, far above capacity. Bound total fallback database reads across instances to at most the safe 500/second, using any lower bound needed for other load. Serve the last known schedule within the permitted 60 seconds only if a usable copy remains accessible outside the unreachable cache. Requests served that copy do no database lookup. Reject requests beyond the fallback allowance with a temporary error when no permitted copy is available; do not fetch anew for each rejected request. After the stale allowance ends, use only bounded database fallback or errors. The lesson supports serving older data but does not specify how to retain it independently during a cache outage, so that availability must be established rather than assumed.

evidence.quote: Many requests miss the same key together and repeat its database lookup. Coalescing requests lets concurrent readers share one in-progress lookup.
Limit fallback work to what the database can handle; reject excess requests or serve older data only where the application permits stale results.

answers.answer: Do not add this cache now. Each unique result is read exactly once with no other readers, so filling the cache after that read creates a copy with no future hit to avoid database work. The database already takes only 2 ms against a 100 ms budget and handles ten reads/second comfortably against 1,000 reads/second capacity. Cache writes, storage, and any cache lookups or maintenance add cost without expected reuse benefit. Reconsider if results begin receiving frequent repeated reads, especially if obtaining them becomes expensive or database load grows, and if an acceptable staleness policy is possible. Then compare response time, database load, hit ratio, and miss cost.

evidence.quote: If requests rarely reuse results, or freshness is too hard to maintain, the cache may cost more than it saves.
Creating the copy still costs work: fetch or compute the result, then write it to the cache.
Choose results that are expensive enough to obtain, frequently reused and able to tolerate a defined amount of staleness.
